title: Ang 885–916: Guru Arjan in Ramkali
hook: some say Ram, some Khuda, on ang 885
tomorrow: what does bliss sound like when it finally comes?

segments.voice: Yesterday, ang 880: two Gurus in one raga, both signing Nanak. Today the fifth Guru takes up Ramkali, with a hymn that sounds like a crowd.
screen: `TWO GURUS, ONE SIGNATURE.` → `THE FIFTH IN RAMKALI.`

segments.voice: Under almost any video about God, the comments fill up with names: God, Allah, Waheguru, Bhagwan, the Universe, and arguments over which one counts. Ang 885 has an odd detail. It's a hymn by Guru Arjan, the fifth Guru, and its center line, the rahao, the pause, calls God Karim and Rahim: the Generous, the Merciful. Those are names from Arabic that Muslims use for God. So what are they doing at the heart of a Sikh hymn?
screen: `THE COMMENTS FULL OF NAMES.` → `THE CENTER LINE: KARIM, RAHIM.` → `WHY HERE?`

segments.voice: Read the whole hymn and the puzzle starts to solve itself. It's a list of people, side by side. In paraphrase: some say Ram, some Khuda. Some serve Gusain, some Allah. Some bathe at holy rivers, some go on Hajj. Some do puja, some bow their heads to the ground. Some read the Vedas, some the Kateb, the books of the prophets. Some wear blue, some white. Some call themselves Turk, some Hindu. Some long for bhisht, some for svarg, two words for paradise. The Guru mocks no line. He doesn't say which side is right. He sets them down like faces around one long table. And in the middle, the pause: the Cause of all causes is Karim; shower your mercy, Rahim. The names the people use become the names in the prayer at the center. Then the last line turns. In paraphrase: says Nanak, whoever recognizes the hukam, the divine order, knows the secret of the Master. Notice what it doesn't say. It doesn't say names don't matter, or that all these practices are secretly one practice. People really do bathe in different rivers and read different books, and the hymn lets them stand. What it asks lives underneath the name: do you see the order the One has set running? The names are many. The secret is in the hukam.
screen: `A LIST OF PEOPLE, SIDE BY SIDE.` · `THE CENTER: KARIM AND RAHIM.` · `THE LAST LINE: THE HUKAM.` · `NOT SAMENESS. ONE ORDER.` · then, large: `MANY NAMES.`

segments.voice: Open to ang 885 if you can, and read the hymn's list out loud, slowly, one pair to a breath: Ram and Khuda, rivers and Hajj, Vedas and Kateb. Then sit in the quiet after the last pair, the way the hymn ends on the hukam rather than on any one name.
Ang 885. Guru Arjan in Ramkali: some say Ram and some Khuda, and the pause at the center calls the One Karim and Rahim.
Many names: every one keeps its seat at the table, and the hymn points under them all to the hukam. Ang 885, read.

howItsDone: Ragis sing Guru Arjan's Ramkali hymns in kirtan; the ang 885 hymn, with its pairs of Hindu and Muslim names and practices, is often explained in katha as a picture of the many ways people call on the One.

fork.setup: your little cousin hears a classmate call God Allah, and asks you: is that the same God or a different one? by the ang 885 hymn, what's your best answer?
options: people call the One by many names; the hymn says what matters is seeing the hukam.

fork.reveal: Guru Arjan sets Ram and Khuda, Gusain and Allah side by side, prays to Karim and Rahim, and ends on the hukam. he doesn't erase the differences; he points beneath them.

original.note: Gurmukhi spelling of Karim, the Generous, a name of God from Arabic, in the rahao of the ang 885 hymn.

trapdoor: what you thought: a Sikh hymn would only use Sikh names for God.
what it means: Guru Arjan lists Ram and Khuda, Gusain and Allah, Hajj and holy rivers, and centers the hymn on Karim and Rahim.

what a scholar hears: the pairs set Persian and Arabic words beside Sanskrit-rooted ones (Kateb and Ved, bhisht and surag), and the last line, hukam pachhaataa, moves the point from the name to the order.

chat.says: maya asked if it's rude to say 'God' instead of waheguru at jas's wedding. is it??
options: Not rude. Guru Arjan's hymn names Ram, Khuda, Allah; it's the hukam that matters.
Inside a gurdwara, say Waheguru; other names belong to other places.
Say anything; the hymn teaches that every religion is exactly the same.
chat.meaning: On ang 885 Guru Arjan sets many names side by side, mocks none, and points to recognizing the hukam, not to one label or to sameness.

Gusain.meaning: a Hindu name for the Lord of the world

Karim.meaning: the Generous, a name of God from Arabic

Rahim.meaning: the Merciful, a name of God from Arabic

hukam.meaning: the divine order, the will that runs through everything

rahao.meaning: the pause: a hymn's center line, its main idea

sources.ref: Ang 885 (Ramkali, Mahala 5: koee bolai raam raam koee khudaae, koee sevai gusaeeaa koee alaahi; rahao: kaaran karan kareem, kirpaa dhaar raheem; last line: kahu naanak jin hukam pachhaataa), paraphrased
